Do Not Restart: Residual Completion for Stateful Agent Handoffs

Runzhi Deng ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Nanjing University Affiliation: Singapore Management University    Yiming Zhong11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Nanjing University    Fang Zhao ††thanks: Corresponding authors. Affiliation: Nanjing University    Pan Zhou22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Singapore Management University
Abstract

Routing and cascades reduce tool-agent cost by transferring control across models, but stateful handoffs must preserve accepted choices, realized effects, and unfinished obligations. We formulate this as commitment-constrained residual completion and introduce Commitment-Frontier Residual Completion (CFRC). CFRC enforces target-before-proposal, whole-proposal-before-authority, and live-evidence-before-success: it freezes a residual contract from accepted progress, closes the successor continuation into an evidence-linked graph, and admits execution only when the remainder is covered, with live receipts discharging obligations. We establish contract-relative partial correctness, which extends to the original residual request under complete contract construction. Across five environments and two same-provider model pairs, CFRC achieves comparable macro accuracy to strong full-task agents at only 22.0%–34.6% of their inference cost, with additional cross-provider results demonstrating broader transfer.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal agents increasingly serve as the decision-making core of tool-using systems for planning, software interaction, and multi-step execution (Trivedi et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). Such trajectories repeatedly invoke a model for reasoning, action selection, tool use, and verification, making it costly and often unnecessary to use the strongest model throughout. A practical alternative is to let lower-cost models handle routine steps and transfer control when tasks become difficult or uncertain (Ong et al., 2024; Son et al., 2026). Its benefit, however, depends on whether the successor can reuse accepted progress rather than restart. Unlike stateless prompt routing (Chen et al., 2023), agents operate in persistent environments where actions can produce irreversible side effects. Restarting wastes computation and risks duplicate actions, while continuing without clear specifications risks goal drift. This raises a broader handoff question: when control passes between models, how can the successor continue from the reached state while preserving accepted choices and realized effects, completing open obligations, and avoiding duplicate actions?

In the invoice task of Fig. 1a, the user asks the agent to pay one outstanding invoice and send its receipt. The first model selects an illustrative invoice INV-42, which the user confirms, making the choice binding even before any tool call. At a later handoff, payment has succeeded but receipt delivery remains pending. The successor cannot restart, as another API payment call would cause a duplicate charge, nor switch invoices, since the user confirmed INV-42. Yet declaring success is also wrong because delivery remains unfulfilled. The task is therefore neither fresh nor complete: the accepted trajectory contains fixed progress alongside unfinished work. We call this handoff point a commitment frontier and frame the challenge as commitment-constrained residual completion. Under this formulation, a valid continuation must execute from the reached state, preserve accepted choices and realized effects, and complete all open request-scoped obligations.

Existing agent components address adjacent parts of this problem but leave three gaps, as illustrated in Fig. 1b. First, routing, handoff, and memory mechanisms determine who acts or transfers past context (KC and Budathoki, 2026; Wang et al., 2024), but they do not independently specify what the successor must still preserve and complete. In the invoice example, transferring the transcript or reached state alone does not prevent the successor from overlooking delivery or reinterpreting the confirmed choice. Second, planners and transcript-conditioned successors can propose later actions (Yao et al., 2023), but a proposal cannot reveal what it omits. A continuation containing only a status check and success response provides no independent signal that receipt delivery remains missing. Third, action-level guards and control layers can reject unsafe or invalid proposed calls (Wang et al., 2026; Kamath et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b), such as duplicate payments or unauthorized invoices. Yet they cannot require an action that was never proposed, nor establish whole-suffix completeness before incremental native execution begins. Thus, existing mechanisms address context transfer, action proposal, or local validity, but not the joint need for an independent residual target, complete proposal coverage, and evidence-backed realization.

Our approach.

We address this gap with Commitment-Frontier Residual Completion (CFRC). The method enforces target before proposal, whole proposal before authority, and live evidence before success, as illustrated in Fig. 1b. First, Reached-State Contract Construction in CFRC derives a frozen residual contract zfz_{f} from the accepted trajectory, reached state, trusted receipts, and public tool interfaces before seeing the successor’s proposal. The contract records what is fixed and what remains open, so omitted work cannot disappear merely because the successor fails to mention it. Second, Executable Residual Completion in CFRC lets the successor author on an isolated replica where available and closes the full continuation as an evidence-linked graph HH, exposing its actions, dependencies, and obligation coverage without changing the live state. Finally, Checked Execution in CFRC admits the complete HH against zfz_{f} before granting native authority, rebinds dynamic values to live predecessor receipts, and accepts completion only when matching native evidence discharges every obligation. In the invoice example, zfz_{f} preserves the completed payment while recording pending delivery; the graph HH must explicitly include that delivery path. Checked Execution rejects duplicate or incomplete proposals before live execution and confirms success only after live receipts verify delivery. Finally, we theoretically establish conditional partial correctness, showing that successfully realized prefixes preserve encoded progress and returned suffixes satisfy the contract.

Across five stateful tool-use surfaces, CFRC shifts the quality–cost frontier (Fig. 1c). With GPT-5.4-mini/GPT-5.5, it achieves 70.8% macro accuracy versus 69.6% for GPT-5.5 at 34.6% of the cost; with Luna/Sol, it achieves 70.8% versus 70.0% at 22.0% cost. Cross-provider Luna/Sonnet 5 and Luna/Gemini 3.7 Flash remain within 0.5 points of their strong anchors at 26.0% and 44.1% cost. Checked Execution blocks invalid proposals before live writes, while an independent audit recovers 62/68 persistent write obligations and finds no ungrounded writes among 50 admitted proposals. So CFRC preserves strong-model quality while focusing expensive reasoning on unfinished work.

2 Related Work

Model routing & agent handoff. Planning and reflection improve how agents generate actions (Yao et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Routers and cascades select models by predicted difficulty or cost (Ong et al., 2024; Bouchard, 2026; Son et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a), while handoff frameworks quantify information loss across checkpoints (KC and Budathoki, 2026). Yet a transferred transcript does not specify which effects are fixed or which obligations remain open. CFRC constructs this residual target before the successor proposes a continuation.

Classical specifications & recovery. Conditional correctness relates execution to explicit pre- and postconditions (Hoare, 1969). Sagas structure long-lived transactions around completion or compensation (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987), while plan repair adapts existing plans to changed execution contexts (Fox et al., 2006). CFRC follows this separation of specification and execution, but constructs the residual target from accepted model-generated progress to constrain the successor’s entire proposal. Accepted effects are preserved, while a failed suffix may return ⊥\bot without compensation.

Stateful control & verification. Runtime guards, capabilities, and transactional frameworks constrain actions outside the model (Wang et al., 2026; Kamath et al., 2025; Debenedetti et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Lin et al., 2026; Patil et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026). Execution-monitoring limits are classical (Schneider, 2000). Our omission argument instead concerns verifying planned coverage before live writes: an incomplete prefix cannot reveal which obligations a future continuation will omit, although explicit terminal obligations can still detect false completion. CFRC checks the entire proposed remainder against a separately constructed target and requires live evidence for success. Stateful benchmarks (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2024; Trivedi et al., 2024; Microsoft, 2026; Pysklo et al., 2026) make the gap between attempted actions and supported completion measurable (Advani, 2026; Gao and Zhou, 2026).

3 Methodology

3.1 Stateful Handoff as a Residual-Completion Problem

Problem setup. A stateful handoff occurs when one model takes over an ongoing tool-use trajectory produced by another, as in routed or cascaded agents for coding, web navigation, and other applications with persistent state or externally visible effects. Unlike a fresh request, the successor inherits both fixed progress that must be preserved and open work that remains to be completed. We study how to finish this residual work without replacing, undoing, or duplicating accepted progress.

Formally, let qq be the original request, τt\tau_{t} the accepted trajectory prefix, sts_{t} the reached live state, and ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} the trusted native receipts available at sts_{t}. Let 𝒜env\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{env}} denote the public tool interfaces, and let 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} denote the semantic, request-scoped obligation instances still open under qq and τt\tau_{t}. We use BtB_{t} for accepted choice bindings, including user-confirmed choices that may precede any native effect, and KtK_{t} for realized effects supported by ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}. With fixed progress Ft=(Bt,Kt)F_{t}=(B_{t},K_{t}), residual completion seeks a continuation σ\sigma from sts_{t} satisfying

Exec⁡(σ,st)∧Preserve⁡(σ,Ft)∧Complete⁡(σ,𝒪t).\mathrm{Exec}(\sigma;s_{t})\;\wedge\;\mathrm{Preserve}(\sigma;F_{t})\;\wedge\;\mathrm{Complete}(\sigma;\mathcal{O}_{t}). (1)

Here, the three predicates require the suffix to execute from the reached state, respect accepted bindings and realized effects, and discharge every open obligation before claiming success. If CFRC cannot establish such a suffix within budget, it returns ⊥\bot; this does not imply that no valid continuation exists. For the formal guarantee, each in-scope obligation has a request-defined, finitely checkable predicate over the resulting trace and state, independent of the contract later constructed by CFRC. Let Σf​(q,τt)\Sigma_{f}(q,\tau_{t}) denote the continuations satisfying Eq. (1).

Running example and commitment frontier. Consider the post-payment invoice handoff in Fig. 2. The request qq asks the agent to pay one outstanding invoice and send its receipt; τt\tau_{t} records that INV-42 was selected and confirmed and that its payment succeeded; sts_{t} contains the paid invoice and receipt file txn7.pdf; and ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} contains the trusted native evidence. Thus, BtB_{t} fixes invoice=INV-42\texttt{invoice}=\texttt{INV-42}, KtK_{t} contains the receipt-backed effect paid⁡(INV-42)\mathrm{paid}(\texttt{INV-42}), and 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t} still requires delivery of the receipt to the verified recipient. A valid σ\sigma may therefore send receipt →\rightarrow verify delivery →\rightarrow confirm success: repaying violates preservation, omitting delivery violates completion, and unsupported success violates Eq. (1). The same issue can arise before any change to the environment: once the user confirms INV-42, that binding already constrains future behavior. We call such a point a commitment frontier: the accepted prefix has fixed progress that must be preserved while request-scoped work remains open—in short, fixed progress plus unfinished work. Before any accepted choice or realized effect, the task is fresh; after all obligations are complete, no residual task remains.

From challenges to CFRC. Eq. (1) exposes three design challenges. (C1) What is fixed, and what remains? Neither the request nor the reached state alone necessarily specifies the residual task, while letting the successor define its own target makes omissions difficult to detect. CFRC therefore constructs an independent frozen contract zfz_{f} before proposal (Sec. 3.2). (C2) Does the proposed remainder cover that target? Call-local checks can reject an invalid action but cannot detect an obligation for which no action is proposed. In stateful environments with irreversible tool mutations, step-by-step execution risks leaving the environment in an unrecoverable state before discovering that downstream obligations lack valid inputs. CFRC therefore exposes the whole remainder as a closed graph HH before native execution (Sec. 3.3). (C3) Were the proposed actions actually realized? Replica results are only proposal-time evidence, and native calls may fail. CFRC therefore grants native authority only after validation and accepts completion only from matching live evidence (Sec. 3.4). These three stages form the pipeline in Fig. 2:

(q,τt,st,ℛt,𝒜env)⟶zf⟶H⟶σ​or⊥.(q,\tau_{t},s_{t},\mathcal{R}_{t},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{env}})\;\longrightarrow\;z_{f}\;\longrightarrow\;H\;\longrightarrow\;\sigma\ \text{or}\ \bot. (2)

We study one handoff tenure at a time. CFRC triggers handoff through a fixed supported-frontier rule, but does not optimize general model routing or choose among multiple successors; it also preserves supported prior commitments rather than re-evaluating their desirability.

3.2 Reached-State Contract Construction

Reached-State Contract Construction (RSCC) addresses C1 in Sec. 3.1 by constructing the residual target before the successor proposes anything. Rather than merely summarize the trajectory, RSCC converts accepted history into a proposal-independent specification of what is fixed and what remains owed. It grounds accepted progress, closes the remaining request, and freezes the resulting contract zfz_{f}. RSCC uses only q,τt,st,ℛtq,\tau_{t},s_{t},\mathcal{R}_{t} and a fixed adapter over public tool schemas. The adapter maps public interfaces into shared argument, effect, and evidence types; it cannot access simulator internals, reference outcomes, or evaluator rewards.

Step 1: Grounding fixed progress. RSCC first identifies the binding parts of the accepted history:

(Bt,Kt,Et)=Ground⁡(τt,st,ℛt),(B_{t},K_{t},E_{t})=\operatorname{Ground}(\tau_{t},s_{t},\mathcal{R}_{t}),

where BtB_{t} contains accepted choice bindings, KtK_{t} contains receipt-backed realized effects that later actions must preserve, and EtE_{t} contains verified entities, values, files, and receipt fields that the residual continuation may safely reference. Grounding is deterministic: public tool schemas specify mutating effects and receipt formats, while Ground\operatorname{Ground} parses trusted native receipts in ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} to populate KtK_{t} and extracts confirmed entities into EtE_{t} and BtB_{t}. In our invoice example, EtE_{t} retains txn7.pdf and the verified recipient, while KtK_{t} records the completed payment.

Step 2: Closing the residual task. Grounding identifies what is fixed but not what remains. RSCC compares the grounded progress with the original request qq and the public interfaces to derive

(τt,st,ℛt)→Ground(Bt,Kt,Et)→𝒜envq,Closezf=(Kt,Et,Ot,𝒮t,𝒜t).\begin{split}(\tau_{t},s_{t},\mathcal{R}_{t})&\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Ground}}(B_{t},K_{t},E_{t})\xrightarrow[\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{env}}]{q,\operatorname{Close}}z_{f}=(K_{t},E_{t},O_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t}).\end{split} (3)

Here, OtO_{t} is the instance-sensitive contract encoding of open obligations 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t}; 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} specifies admissible residual effects, and 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} the interfaces that may realize or verify them. Closure operationalizes the division of labor between rules and model inference. On structured surfaces (STATE-Bench, ToolSandbox, Agent-Diff), candidate obligations are extracted deterministically by matching request intents against tool schemas and excluding effects already certified in KtK_{t}. On conversational surfaces (τ2\tau^{2}), an extraction prompt decomposes user request qq relative to prefix τt\tau_{t} into candidate obligations OtO_{t}, parameterizing them with entities from EtE_{t} and restricting them to admissible interfaces 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}. For the post-payment invoice, OtO_{t} encodes delivery of txn7.pdf to the verified recipient, 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} permits delivery and receipt-backed confirmation while excluding repayment, and 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} retains the corresponding send and status interfaces. Accepted bindings in BtB_{t} are compiled into fixed values in EtE_{t}, obligations in OtO_{t}, and restrictions in 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t}, while receipt-backed effects in KtK_{t} remain protected against reversal or repetition.

Step 3: Validating and freezing the contract. RSCC requires every contract field to have trusted support, OtO_{t} to be nonempty, and the accepted prefix to contain at least one supported accepted binding or receipt-backed realized effect. Once validated, zfz_{f} is frozen before querying the successor: neither proposal nor execution may expand, weaken, or rewrite it, so recorded work cannot disappear because the successor omits it. These checks establish support but do not prove that RSCC captured every semantic obligation in 𝒪t\mathcal{O}_{t}. Freezing prevents proposal-induced omission; it cannot recover an obligation missed during construction. Accordingly, the lift from contract-relative correctness to the original residual request is conditional on complete RSCC construction (Sec. 3.5). If construction or validation fails, CFRC withholds successor write authority and returns ⊥\bot.

3.3 Executable Residual Completion

The frozen contract zfz_{f} specifies what must be preserved and completed while leaving how to the successor. ERC addresses C2 in Sec. 3.1 by exposing the successor’s complete proposed remainder before any new live write: the successor authors a continuation, a deterministic bridge binds its data and evidence dependencies, and the proposal is closed as an untrusted graph HH.

Step 1: Data-dependent authoring without live effects. Residual plans are often data-dependent because later call arguments depend on earlier outputs. When safe snapshotting is available, the successor authors against an isolated replica of sts_{t}, observing replica receipts ρ~v\widetilde{\rho}_{v} without changing the live environment. On an unforkable surface, the successor instead closes the graph from handoff-time evidence and symbolic receipt dependencies; no new state-changing live call is authorized before CE in Sec. 3.4 admits the complete proposal. Replica receipts may expose intermediate values for authoring, but they neither prove live effects nor discharge obligations. For example, the successor may send txn7.pdf on a replica, observe a SEND receipt, and use its identifier to propose a later delivery-status query without sending a real email.

Step 2: Binding dependencies and closing the residual graph. A proposal authored from replica values cannot simply be replayed because replica-generated identifiers may differ from live ones.

A deterministic bridge therefore builds an evidence-linked candidate graph. Let HH denote the closed DAG retained after any dependency-closed compiler selection, containing typed calls, the terminal response, arguments, dependencies, source bindings, obligation coverage, effects, and required authority.

Crucially, dynamic arguments bind to their source, not to a proposal-time value. For example, the status query refers to the send_id field of the preceding SEND receipt; CE (Sec. 3.4) later resolves that field from the corresponding live receipt. The successor chooses the actions, task-specific arguments, semantic order, and terminal response. The bridge only records or normalizes structure supported by zfz_{f}, public schemas, and available receipts; it does not choose another task solution.

Step 3: Closing the whole remainder without repair. Unlike next-action control, HH exposes the entire proposed remainder. Writing cov⁡(v)\operatorname{cov}(v) for the obligations claimed by node vv,

cov⁡(H)=⋃v∈V⁡(H)cov⁡(v),\operatorname{cov}(H)=\bigcup\nolimits_{v\in V(H)}\operatorname{cov}(v), (4)

can later be compared with OtO_{t}. Thus an omitted action becomes visible as missing coverage: an invoice proposal without a SEND node leaves receipt delivery uncovered.

Crucially, while a terminal monitor can detect omission at episode end, it cannot roll back irreversible tool mutations already committed to the live environment. Nor can step-by-step checkers observe whether future actions will complete open obligations. Closing HH beforehand validates full obligation coverage and dataflow reachability before granting live write authority, preventing destructive partial execution. The bridge does not repair the proposal; it normalizes supported dependencies, source bindings, or coverage annotations without adding, removing, or replacing task actions. The resulting HH is inspectable but untrusted.

3.4 Checked Execution

The closed HH from Sec. 3.3 makes the successor’s proposal explicit but does not establish that it is contract-valid or that its claimed effects actually occur. Checked Execution (CE) resolves C3 by putting state-changing live authority behind whole-graph admission and accepting completion only from live evidence. CE first admits HH against zfz_{f}, then realizes admitted nodes using live receipt bindings, and finally verifies that the resulting evidence discharges every obligation.

Step 1: Whole-graph admission before live write authority. Before the first state-changing native call, CE compares the fixed proposal HH with zf=(Kt,Et,Ot,𝒮t,𝒜t)z_{f}=(K_{t},E_{t},O_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t}). Admission requires: (i) calls use allowed interfaces with well-typed, grounded arguments; (ii) proposed effects stay within 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} and preserve KtK_{t} and the accepted bindings encoded by the contract; (iii) the entire graph covers the encoded obligations, cov⁡(H)=Ot\operatorname{cov}(H)=O_{t}; and (iv) dependencies and terminal claims have explicit evidence paths. These conditions correspond to proposal-level executability, preservation, and coverage. Because CE sees the complete HH, it can reject duplicate actions, uncovered obligations, unresolved dependencies, or unsupported terminal claims before the first live write. Whole-graph admission establishes that the planned suffix satisfies the contract structure; it does not imply that native execution will succeed. CE admits or rejects the selected HH as a whole. Compiler selection may prune proposal nodes only while retaining dependencies and full coverage of OtO_{t}; it cannot synthesize repair actions.

Step 2: Receipt-bound live realization. An admitted graph executes in dependency order on the live environment. Static inputs resolve from EtE_{t}, whereas dynamic inputs are rebound to the corresponding live predecessor receipts specified by HH. After each call, CE checks the returned receipt against the result and effect instance recorded for that node before its fields may feed downstream calls. Replica and proposal-time outputs never substitute for native evidence.

Step 3: Evidence-backed completion. Replica success never discharges an obligation. Let sjs_{j} and ℛj\mathcal{R}_{j} denote the live state and matching native receipts after jj successfully realized action nodes. CE tracks the obligations whose evidence remains valid at that point:

Lj={o∈Ot:witj⁡(o,ℛj,sj)},L0=∅,L_{j}=\{\,o\in O_{t}:\operatorname{wit}_{j}(o,\mathcal{R}_{j},s_{j})\,\},\qquad L_{0}=\varnothing, (5)

where witj\operatorname{wit}_{j} requires instance-matching native evidence whose discharge remains valid at sjs_{j}. Event obligations may remain discharged once witnessed; mutable-state obligations require current-state validity. Recorded invalidation removes discharge and blocks completion for the current tenure; a fresh receipt cannot discharge that obligation again under the same contract.

If mm action nodes are realized, CE returns a suffix σ\sigma only when every node has a matching receipt, Lm=OtL_{m}=O_{t}, and the terminal response is supported by the corresponding evidence:

Γzf​(H)={σ,if admission and all live-evidence checks succeed,⊥,otherwise.\Gamma_{z_{f}}(H)=\begin{cases}\sigma,&\text{if admission and all live-evidence checks succeed},\\ \bot,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (6)

A rejection before live execution may trigger another complete proposal against the same frozen contract within budget. Once a state-changing live call has occurred, however, a failure or mismatched receipt ends the current tenure; CE does not repair the old graph or continue under stale contract evidence. A later attempt reconstructs a contract from the new reached state. Importantly, ⊥\bot after a live call does not imply rollback or that the environment remained unchanged.

3.5 Conditional End-to-End Guarantee

The three stages establish complementary properties: Under complete construction, RSCC faithfully specifies the residual task; ERC exposes the successor’s proposal without repairing it, and CE faithfully realizes an admitted proposal using live evidence.

Proposition 1 (Contract-relative partial correctness and residual-task lift).

Let PP be a successor-authored residual proposal and H=ERCzf⁡(P)H=\operatorname{ERC}_{z_{f}}(P) its closed graph. Under faithful ERC closure, sound schemas and checks, valid live evidence, and tenure isolation, if Γzf(H)=σ≠⊥\Gamma_{z_{f}}(H)=\sigma\neq\bot, then every successfully realized prefix preserves the frozen progress and

cov⁡(H)=Ot,σ∈Σ⁡(zf).\operatorname{cov}(H)=O_{t},\qquad\sigma\in\Sigma(z_{f}). (7)

If RSCC satisfies the complete-construction assumption, then σ∈Σf​(q,τt)\sigma\in\Sigma_{f}(q,\tau_{t}) and satisfies Eq. (1).

Proposition 1 separates execution fidelity from specification fidelity. Under the assumptions stated in Proposition 1, ERC and CE ensure that the returned suffix satisfies the frozen contract: the closed graph covers every encoded obligation, each successfully realized prefix preserves encoded progress, and live evidence supports completion. Under complete RSCC construction, this contract-relative result lifts to the original in-scope residual request. The returned suffix therefore executes from the reached state, preserves accepted progress, and completes every in-scope semantic obligation still open at handoff. The result does not certify the constructor, guarantee that a valid proposal will be found, or imply rollback when ⊥\bot is returned.

4 Experiments

Our evaluation investigates four questions: whether CFRC approaches strong-model quality at lower inference cost, whether these gains hold across model pairs and providers, what RSCC, ERC, and CE individually contribute, and whether independent audits validate the contract and execution mechanisms.

Surfaces and protocol. We evaluate across five stateful tool-use benchmarks, comprising STATE-Bench, τ2\tau^{2}-Retail, τ2\tau^{2}-Airline, ToolSandbox, and Agent-Diff (Microsoft, 2026; Barres et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2024; Pysklo et al., 2026). All methods use the same frozen tasks, public tool environment, and scorer. CFRC accesses only public action schemas, effect types, and native receipts, without simulator internals, reference outputs, or evaluator rewards.

Models and baselines. Our primary evaluations use GPT-5.4-mini/GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna/Sol; three cross-provider pairs test transfer. Baselines include cheap and strong full-task agents, StepWise, MTRouter, RouteLLM-BERT, FrugalGPT, and AgServe-QAC (Wei et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Ong et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2025). Policies and operating points are fixed before test evaluation.

Metrics and cost. We report official task success except for ToolSandbox, whose metric is strict all-milestone completion. Cost is cache-neutral provider expenditure over all agent calls, excluding user-simulator and evaluator roles. Aggregates are computed over each method’s evaluated surfaces.

4.1 End-to-End Quality and Cost

Macro quality vs. strong anchors. In Table 1, CFRC matches strong anchors within 1.2 points on macro average under GPT-5.4-mini/GPT-5.5 at 34.6% mean cost, and within 0.9 points under Luna/Sol at 22.0% cost. GPT-5.4-mini/GPT-5.5 matches or exceeds strong anchors on four surfaces, trailing by 2.0 points on Airline; Luna/Sol ties or exceeds on three surfaces, trailing by 3.5 and 3.2 points on Retail and Airline. Across five runs, CFRC macro standard deviations are 0.54 and 0.58 points, reflecting comparable macro quality rather than uniform dominance.

Comparison with routing and cascades. RouteLLM-BERT and FrugalGPT trail GPT-5.5 by 2.1 and 1.3 points at 59.7% and 96.3% cost, while CFRC gains 1.2 points at 34.6% cost. On StepWise, AgServe-QAC, and MTRouter subsets, CFRC improves accuracy by 3.3, 7.1, and 6.3 points while cutting cost by 37–49%, showing the benefit of preserving progress over simple call reduction.

Cross-provider transfer. Luna/Sonnet 5 and Luna/Gemini 3.7 Flash match strong anchors within 0.5 points macro completion at 26.0% and 44.1% cost across five benchmarks, though ToolSandbox similarity softens under Gemini. Haiku 4.5/Sol trails Sol by 5.0 points at 57.4% cost because weaker cheap prefixes introduce flawed commitments, though CFRC gains 17.0 points over the cheap anchor.

4.2 Validating the Three Stages

Stage-wise progression across components. Table 2 isolates post-frontier mechanisms from captured state sts_{t}. Direct Takeover achieves 58.9% accuracy at $68.82 from exploratory wander. Certified Direct supplies frozen contracts via RSCC but retains incremental action checking, reaching 62.0% at $47.06. Contract Plan adds replica authoring to reach 65.4%, and Full CFRC adds Checked Execution to reach 70.8% at $38.80. Comparing Full CFRC against Certified Direct shows that gating writes behind whole-graph admission adds 8.8 points and saves $8.26 over step-by-step checking under the same contract by preventing destructive partial execution.

Where cost is spent. Table 3 decomposes the $38.80 spend, where RSCC averages $0.21 across surfaces. Three call mechanisms drive the 43.6% savings over Direct Takeover. Selective invocation restricts strong calls to post-frontier residuals, engaging on 59.6% of episodes. RSCC eliminates exploratory re-querying with grounded obligations, and CE fail-closed checks halt ungrounded plans early to prevent runaway retries.

4.3 Auditing Contracts and Checked Execution

Contract adequacy. Table 4 grounds all 50 audited bindings and recovers 62 of 68 persistent write obligations, achieving 91.2% recall. No ungrounded live writes were admitted in the audited sample of 50 candidate proposals, corresponding to an exact Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound of 5.8%. Six omissions involved implicit updates without entity mentions; four were blocked downstream and two yielded false completions. Formal lift to the residual objective remains conditional on complete construction because conversational disclosures fall outside tool schemas.

Checked Execution as an authority boundary. Table 4 shows that all 124 CE interventions occur before the first live write. These comprise 43 active proposal rejections, spanning 25 coverage, 10 dependency, and 8 grounding failures, alongside 81 holds. All 43 rejections reproduce under deterministic replay.

5 Conclusion

We formalize stateful agent handoff as commitment-constrained residual completion and introduce CFRC, freezing residual contracts from accepted history, authoring closed graphs on replicas, and verifying execution via live receipts. Across five surfaces and model pairings, CFRC matches strong full-task quality at a fraction of inference cost while blocking unadmitted mutations.

Scope and limitations. We evaluate single-tenure cheap-to-strong handoffs under frozen contracts. While multi-tier cascades readily compose with CFRC, recursive routing policies lie beyond our immediate scope. Formal lift to the residual task remains conditional on complete RSCC construction, as conversational disclosures fall outside tool-effect schemas.

Reproducibility statement. Code and schemas will be open-sourced.
